generatedCommentsNodes.comment: The FLS test asserts only on the column structure (which fields are visible) but never checks the returned `values`. Since the `other` field has no indexed data, all values would be `null`, making a value assertion low-value here. However, for `fls_user2` and `fls_user4`, the `org` column *does* have data (e.g., `"sales"` for `x=40.0`). Adding a value assertion (e.g., `assertThat(respMap.get("values"), equalTo(List.of(List.of(40.0, 40.0, "sales"))))`) would guard against a regression where the correct columns are reported but the underlying join produces wrong or missing values.

The LOOKUP-mode validation (single-index check, mode check) was moved from `resolveIndex` (analysis phase) to `LookupJoin.postAnalysisVerification` (post-analysis phase). This is a reasonable centralization, but it has a side effect: during analysis, an `EsRelation` is now constructed for LOOKUP-mode targets even when they resolve to multiple indices or a non-LOOKUP-mode index. Any code that inspects the plan between analysis and post-analysis verification (e.g., plan serialization, metrics collection, or other visitors) will see a structurally valid `EsRelation` where previously it would have seen an `UnresolvedRelation`. If no such intermediate consumers exist, this is fine; otherwise, the error surface shifts from "unresolved index" to "post-analysis failure," which may be less intuitive for users reading error messages.

Sorry, one last test suggestion - we can also add this in a separate PR if you're already about to make this ready to merge.

I just noticed: all of the fls test cases have permission to read the `value` field, which is the join key.

I think it'd be interesting to test if forbidding this field for a user makes it so all look ups are null. And, if we wanna be extra paranoid, consider the case where the lookup index has duplicates for a given join key, so the `LOOKUP JOIN` would lead to extra rows - but without permissions granted on the join key, no extra rows should be emitted. (Otherwise, users could exfiltrate statistics about fields they have no permissions on).

Thanks Alex, I still have a couple of things to push, I'll add this one as well.
I _think_ the whole query will fail because the user doesn't see the join key in the schema, but I'll double-check
The new tests confirm the above: if a role cannot see the join key in the lookup index, the query will fail with "Unknown column"
